CHIEF COMPLAINT
Annual exam.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Ralph is a 62-year-old male with a history of depression, prior lobectomy, and hypertension, presenting for his annual exam. He reports feeling relatively okay, though he experienced a stressful spring with allergies/pollen and moving his oldest daughter into her college dorm. His depression is well-managed on Prozac, and he has stayed on top of his medications without incidents. His hypertension has been a bit more of a struggle; he is regular with Norvasc during the business week, but sometimes forgets it on the weekends when he is on the go. He reports some nasal congestion from pollen. He runs 4 to 5 miles a day and notes that in relative humidity, he struggles a little bit with some shortness of breath upon exertion and a little pounding in his chest that usually goes away. 

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Endorsed nasal congestion from pollen, and shortness of breath with exertion/running in humid weather. Denies cough, or muscle aches. (Note: other elements reviewed via nurse's sheet).

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Blood pressure in the office today is 120/80. 
Heart: Regular rate and rhythm; 2/6 systolic ejection murmur noted.
Lungs: Clear to auscultation; no lower extremity edema. 
Sinuses: Pain to palpation of the sinuses.

RESULTS
EKG: Completely normal.
Chest X-ray: Looks really good, normal, no issues related to prior lobectomy.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Depression: Doing well on current strategy. Continue Prozac 20 mg daily. Refill ordered.
2. Prior lobectomy / Shortness of breath: No further workup needed; exercise capacity is high (running 4-5 miles/day). No need to follow up with the surgeon.
3. Hypertension: Well-controlled. Continue current Norvasc medication. 
4. Systolic murmur / Chest pounding: Order an echocardiogram to evaluate the murmur; follow up with results.
5. Routine blood work to be ordered, with results communicated via the patient portal.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Fatigue, lightheadedness, and feeling out of sorts for about 5 weeks.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a 58-year-old male with a past medical history of congestive heart failure and hypertension who presents for follow-up of his chronic problems. He reports feeling out of sorts, lacking energy, tired, fatigued, and experiencing occasional lightheadedness starting around Labor Day (about 5 weeks ago). He notes occasional bloating and some shortness of breath when exerting energy on home projects. He reports slight chest cramps that go away after about an hour, and a slight cough. He denies fevers, chills, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. He reports taking his medications, but notes his diet has been off since starting kitchen renovations over Labor Day weekend, leading to eating out more frequently. He monitors his blood pressure regularly at home with a cuff and assistance from his wife.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Positive for fatigue, lightheadedness, occasional bloating, shortness of breath with exertion, slight chest cramps, and a slight cough. Negative for fevers, chills, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: Blood pressure, heart rate, and oxygenation look good in the office.
Neck: Jugular venous distention to about 8 cm.
Heart: 3/6 systolic ejection murmur.
Lungs: Fine crackles at the bases bilaterally.
Extremities: 1+ pitting edema in the lower extremities.

RESULTS
Chest X-ray: Shows a little bit of fluid in the lungs, attributed to heart failure.
Echocardiogram (from about 4 months ago): Shows pumping function of the heart is a little bit reduced at 45%, and mitral regurgitation (leaky valve).

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Congestive heart failure: Patient is retaining fluid. Increase Lasix to 80 mg once a day. Weigh daily and call if gaining weight or experiencing shortness of breath. Order a repeat echocardiogram.
2. Hypertension: Managing well at this time. Continue lisinopril 20 mg a day. Continue to record blood pressures at home and report elevations via the patient portal.

Right finger pain.

Sharon Brooks is a 48-year-old female presenting for right finger pain. She was skiing over the weekend on Sunday and tried moguls, where her strap got caught on her finger and bent it back. Not discussed.

Tenderness over the distal phalanx (the tip of the finger) and over the joint itself. No tenderness over the proximal joint or the metacarpophalangeal joint (above the knuckle). Able to bend the finger, extend it, and touch the thumb with it.

X-ray of the right finger is normal with no fractures; everything lines up well.

Diagnosis: Right hand index finger contusion on the tip of the finger.
Plan: 
- Aluminum foam splint.
- Motrin 600 mg every six hours for about a week.
- Follow up and call if it does not get better.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Long-standing iron deficiency anemia.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Christina Cooper is a 65-year-old female referred by Dr. Diane Nelson for long-standing iron deficiency anemia, dating back to when she was 13 years old. The patient recently tried to donate blood in December and was told she was anemic. She reports feeling fatigued during the day, feverish with chills at times, shortness of breath and wheezing with activity, headaches, chilling sensations, and feeling cold easily. She also notes worsening anxiety and depression. She had heavy periods in the past until a hysterectomy in 1996. Her last colonoscopy was about 5 to 6 years ago and was reported as normal with no polyps. She recently restarted taking ferrous sulfate 25 mg tablets twice daily and over-the-counter vitamin B12.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General: Fatigue, feverish with chills at times, chilling sensations, feels cold easily.
Respiratory: Shortness of breath and wheezing with activity.
Neurological: Headaches.
Psychiatric: Worsening anxiety and depression.
All other systems were reviewed and are otherwise negative.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Pleasant 65-year-old female.
Heart: Normal.
Lungs: Normal.
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender, no tenderness to palpation.
Overall physical exam is normal without any significant findings.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Iron deficiency anemia: 
   - Continue ferrous sulfate 25 mg twice daily, now instructed to take with orange juice (vitamin C) to improve absorption for 8-12 weeks, then reassess blood work (CBC, iron, ferritin, B12, and folate).
   - Schedule upper endoscopy (EGD) and colonoscopy to assess for potential sources of anemia or GI bleed.
   - If EGD and colonoscopy are inconclusive, consider a capsule endoscopy.
2. Hematology referral: 
   - Send a referral to Dr. Flores (hematologist) for evaluation regarding potential IV iron or other therapies.
3. Patient instructed to call with questions or worsening symptoms and to schedule the recommended procedures and specialist appointment upon checkout.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Chest pain, fall, and shortness of breath following an emergency department visit.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a male seen via telehealth following a recent emergency department visit. He reports he was outside walking, fell down, and experienced chest pain which he attributed to a pulled muscle or heartburn, and shortness of breath, which he initially brushed off. He admits to missing his blood pressure medications every now and then, noting he only took one today. He reports his diet has been poor, consuming salty foods like chips, especially around the holidays. He currently reports feeling a little out of breath, but nothing he cannot handle. He has not yet purchased a home blood pressure cuff. 

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General: Denies major complaints other than feeling a little out of breath. 
Cardiovascular: Reports slight chest pain here or there, attributed to heartburn. Reports history of hypertension and recent ankle swelling.
Respiratory: Reports shortness of breath when walking outside. 
Sleep: Denies problems sleeping ("sleep like a rock").
All other systems reviewed and negative except as noted.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital Signs: Blood pressure 128/72 mmHg. Other vital signs look good. (Note: ER blood pressure was noted earlier as 200/90).
Neck: No jugular venous distention.
Heart: 2/6 systolic ejection murmur, previously noted and stable.
Lungs: Clear bilaterally.
Extremities: Trace edema in lower extremities.

RESULTS
Echocardiogram (from ER): Preserved ejection fraction of 55%, normal diastolic filling, and mild to moderate mitral regurgitation.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Congestive Heart Failure (CHF): Likely precipitated by dietary indiscretion and uncontrolled hypertension. 
   - Continue Bumex 2 mg once daily. Ensure consistent medication adherence.
   - Get a scale and weigh daily. Call if weight gain is 3 pounds in 2 days.
   - Consult nutrition for dietary advice, specifically regarding sodium intake.
2. Hypertension: Uncontrolled, related to medication non-adherence and diet.
   - Continue Cozaar 100 mg daily.
   - Continue Norvasc 5 mg once daily.
   - Obtain a blood pressure cuff for home monitoring and track blood pressures.
   - Order renal artery ultrasound to evaluate further.
3. Tobacco Use: Stopped smoking a couple of years ago, but admits to occasional relapse (about one cigarette every week). Encourage continuation of smoking cessation.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Sharp pain on the right side of the abdomen below the ribs for the last several days.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Russell is a male presenting with sharp pain on the right side of his abdomen below the ribs for the last several days. The pain radiates to the lower abdomen and into the groin. It comes and goes, is pretty bad when present, and prevents him from finding a comfortable position. He reports mild burning with urination and urine that looks a little dark sometimes, but no frank blood. He has taken Tylenol without much relief. He feels nauseated but has not vomited. He reports a family history of kidney stones (father) and a personal history of prior kidney stones that he was able to pass, though this current episode is taking much longer.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Negative for fever and chills. Nausea present, negative for vomiting.
Genitourinary: Burning with urination, urine looks a little dark sometimes, no frank blood.
All other systems not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Abdomen: No tenderness to palpation, no evidence of rebound or guarding, no peritoneal signs. 
Flank: Positive CVA tenderness on the right flank.

RESULTS
CT scan of the abdomen (ordered by primary care doctor): Shows a 0.5 cm kidney stone located in the proximal right ureter. No evidence of hydronephrosis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Acute nephrolithiasis (kidney stone):
- Recommend pushing fluids to help facilitate urination and pass the stone.
- Prescribe oxycodone 5 mg every 6 to 8 hours as needed for pain; may continue to alternate with Tylenol.
- Provide a urine strainer to catch the stone for analysis if it passes.
- Order a basic metabolic panel, urinalysis, and urine culture.
- Discussed potential further treatments if symptoms persist, including lithotripsy or ureteroscopy.
- Follow-up in 1 to 2 weeks, or sooner if symptoms worsen.

Negative for numbness or tingling in the arms or hands. Otherwise, not discussed.

Vitals: Reviewed, all look good.
Left Shoulder: Limited active and passive range of motion. Tender to palpation at the greater tuberosity of the humerus. No tenderness at the sternoclavicular or acromioclavicular joints. 
Extremities: Good hand grips.
Neurovascular (Left Arm): Capillary refill is less than three seconds. Sensation is intact to light touch.

RESULTS
Left shoulder X-ray reviewed: No fractures.

- Continue taking Tylenol as needed for pain.
- Discussed potential future consideration of a steroid injection if symptoms do not improve.

- Schedule a follow-up visit after completion of physical therapy.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Worsening headaches and a newly diagnosed pituitary lesion.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a 52-year-old male with a newly diagnosed pituitary lesion, seen in consultation at the request of Dr. Henry Howard for possible surgical intervention. The patient presented to Dr. Howard on 3/1/21 complaining of worsening headaches over the past few months. He denied any previous trouble with headaches. The headaches started about three months ago, located behind the eyes, described as a dull nagging ache. They began at a severity of 3/10 and gradually worsened to 6/10. They tend to be worse in the morning, last a few hours at a time, and nothing makes them better or worse. He tried Tylenol a few times without relief and stopped. He reports recently bumping into door frames. He denies fever, illness, rash, neck issues, numbness, tingling, weakness, passing out, or changes in balance. 

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No fever or feeling sick. 
Skin: No rashes. 
Neurological: Complains of worsening headaches and bumping into door frames. No neck issues, numbness, tingling, weakness, or passing out. 
All other systems reviewed and are negative.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
The patient is alert, oriented to time, place, and person. Affect is appropriate and speech is fluent. Cranial nerve examination is grossly intact. No focal, motor, or sensory deficit in the upper or lower extremities. Visual acuity and eye movements are normal. Pupils are equal and reactive. Visual field testing reveals bitemporal hemianopia. Color vision is normal.

RESULTS
Labs dated 3/3/21 (CBC, unet/unes, coagulation, and CRP) were normal. Pituitary hormone profile demonstrates a low TSH; all other results were normal. MRI of the brain with contrast from 3/4/21 reveals a pituitary lesion with elevation and compression of the optic chiasm. Ventricles are normal in size, and no other abnormalities are noted.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Diagnosis: Pituitary adenoma (benign-appearing pituitary adenoma with clinical and radiographical evidence of optic chiasmal compression).
Plan:
1. Surgical intervention via a minimally invasive transsphenoidal approach to excise and decompress the pituitary fossa is indicated. Discussed risks of anesthesia and surgery.
2. Referral to ophthalmology for a full exam and formal visual field test to map peripheral/side vision prior to surgery and monitor post-operatively.
3. The patient will meet with the surgery scheduler, Deborah, on the way out to schedule the surgery and the pre-surgery visual field test.
4. The removed adenoma will be sent to pathology to confirm the diagnosis.

- Rest the right elbow.
- Order a sling to be worn while awake.
- Apply ice to the elbow for 20 minutes three times a day.
- Take ibuprofen 600 mg Q6H with food for a full week.
- Hold off on pottery work for the next couple of weeks.
- Follow-up visit in one week.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Left knee pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a female presenting with left knee pain that occurs occasionally, less than once a day when walking. She reports that the knee feels like it "gives out" and she thinks she is going to fall, though she usually catches herself or holds a grocery cart. The episodes pass as quickly as they come. She denies hearing or feeling a pop and denies any known injury or fall to the knee. She does not take anything for pain because it does not last long. The pain is not really interfering with things she likes to do, though she has an upcoming trip to Georgia with a Lions Club function where she expects to do a lot of walking, and she is deciding not to participate in line dancing to avoid taking a chance on her knee. 

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Blood sugars have been running a little higher at about 130 fasting in the morning. Blood pressure has been running around 120/70 and is reported to be doing fine. Medications are taken regularly at 8:30 AM and 8:30 PM. 

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
- Vital Signs: Temperature 98.2, pulse 72, respirations 16, blood pressure 122/70.
- Cardiovascular: Nice regular rate and rhythm; faint 2/6 systolic ejection murmur at the left base.
- Pulmonary: Lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally.
- Left Knee / Extremities: No ecchymosis or edema, no effusion, no pain to palpation of the left medial knee. Can bend and straighten the knee. No decreased range of motion. Negative varus and valgus tests. 

RESULTS
Left knee x-ray reviewed: showed no evidence of fracture or bony abnormality.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Left knee pain / suspected arthritis: Prescribe meloxicam 15 mg daily. Consider physical therapy to strengthen muscles around the area and prevent further problems.
2. Hypertension: Continue lisinopril at 20 mg daily. Order an echocardiogram to evaluate the heart murmur.
3. Diabetes mellitus: Order a hemoglobin A1c to evaluate if adjustments to metformin are needed. Order a lipid panel.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right knee pain and hypertension follow-up.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Philip is a male presenting with right knee pain that started one week ago after he slipped and fell while doing work on his property. He felt something pop when the injury occurred and reports the knee became a little bit swollen. He notes pain when flexing and extending the knee and when putting pressure on it. Pain score is 4 to 5 out of 10 with mobility, and none when stationary. He has been taking ibuprofen for swelling. 

For his hypertension, he reports taking his lisinopril 20 mg regularly. He admits his diet got out of control during the pandemic and he has not made changes to reduce his sodium intake to 2300 mg per day. His blood pressure today in the office was 150/70.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General: Not discussed.
Chest pain: Negative.
Shortness of breath: Negative.
Belly pain: Negative.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Blood pressure 150/70.
Lungs: Clear bilaterally, no wheezes or crackles.
Heart: Grade 2/6 systolic ejection murmur.
Right Knee Exam: Pain to palpation of the medial aspect of the right knee. No pain on the outside. Pain with flexion and extension. Edema around the knee and effusion/fluid present.

RESULTS
Right knee X-ray: No fractures, no bony abnormalities.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Right medial collateral ligament (MCL) strain, secondary to fall and twist one week ago.
   - Prescribe ibuprofen 800 mg, take twice a day for pain and swelling.
   - Place patient in a knee brace to support muscles and allow healing.
   - Ice the knee for 20 minutes at a time, 3 to 4 times a day to help with swelling.
   - Elevate the leg and stay off the leg for a couple of weeks.
2. Hypertension.
   - Continue lisinopril 20 mg daily.
   - Provide referral to nutrition to help with diet and sodium reduction, with the goal of eventually reducing/stopping medication.
